speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in taking part in this debate I should like to say a few words about the Minister of Agriculture himself. His constituency adjoins mine, and no matter what side of the house we may be on I think that as members of parliament and representatives of the people of Canada we will all agree that the portfolio of agriculture is not an easy one. The big trouble in dealing with agriculture is that it is like the seven blind men feeling various parts of the elephant which all feel different to them. Agriculture covers so many different items, so many different crops, so many different phases that when you cure one problem you may aggravate something else.
I certainly do not want to get into an argument with the last speaker but he mentioned that there had been a lot said in this debate and he thought there must be something wrong. I would say there is nothing wrong and as a member from western Canada I say there should be a lot of words spoken about agriculture because that is our primary industry. That is how all of us make a living because when the farmer in western Canada does well the businessmen of western Canada also do well.
I should like to deal with a few things that concern my province and constituency having to do with a phase of agriculture called ranching. Sometimes Albertans are accused
EMr. Howard.]
of being a lot like Texans but they can boast about having some of the Anest ranches in Canada. I can tell members who have not visited the area that in the foothhills of the Rocky mountains they will And some of the Anest herds of cattle you will see anywhere in Canada and a pound of beef can probably be produced cheaper there than anywhere else in Canada because in many places the cattle can graze all year round.
Therefore, when legislation is brought in or a program is suggested with reference to the production of cattle, what may apply to one section of the country may not apply to another. In many places in Canada, even in some sections of Alberta, cattle have to be barn fed for six or seven months of the year. The people who have to barn feed their cattle are faced with tough competition from the rancher because the rancher's cattle can graze for most of the year.
There is one matter that is of considerable concern to Alberta ranchers at this time, and that is what may happen as a result of diversiAcation in farming. I have discussed the matter with ranchers and many members have suggested that the farmers of western Canada should diversify their production. In the process of diversiAcation many of them have gone into raising cattle. In the last two years at least we have been very fortunate to have a good market for our cattle in the United States. This means, of course, that every ranch is producing every pound of beef possible and where there has been diversiAcation on farms there is also a lot of beef being produced.
There is always a danger when there is overproduction and there is the problem of what will happen if the United States market is cut off. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe referred to the situation when our market for cattle in the United States was cut off in 1920 and 1930. We know exactly what happened to cattle prices in Canada. It is a source of anxiety to the ranchers and other cattle producers of Canada to know that if this market is cut off they will be faced with an immediate problem. However, it bears repeating to refer again to the stabilization legislation. It is sometimes underemphasized that under that legislation there are two price levels. One price is written right into the act and cannot be changed except by act of parliament. It is provided right in the act that the price will never fall below 80 per cent of a 10-year moving average. That

is a matter of law and cannot be changed. Then there is the other level which comes into effect when a price level is set for a product by the stabilization board. That has given the ranchers and other cattle producers of Alberta stability and security in their industry and it is something that I think should be mentioned.
There is one thing that I should like to suggest to the Minister of Agriculture and also to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Members of parliament will have read about the recent case in British Columbia, I believe, in which the wheat board act and the regulations were interpreted to mean that wheat could not be sold by one farmer in one province to another farmer in another province. This has worked certain hardship, particularly in the case of those farmers who live near the border between Saskatchewan and Alberta. Some of the wheat which cannot be sold under the quota system is sold for feed and bought by feeders of cattle and in that way the surplus is being depleted. But under the wheat board regulations it is legally impossible to sell wheat from one province to another without at least the consent of the wheat board or rather through the wheat board. That is one of the big problems and I think it should be looked into because it does seem that when we provide certain protection for an industry by legislation problems always arise.
The wheat board is not new, of course, because the board was created by this party the last time it was in power, but I always think that new legislation is like a new baby. There are certain changes that must take place. I should like to make this suggestion in respect of this legislation without wanting in any way to harm the sytsem itself whereby the wheat farmer is protected. Perhaps some system could be worked out whereby the law and these regulations could be amended to enable a farmer in one province to sell grain to a farmer in another province. I know of a case in which a man in Saskatchewan wanted to sell wheat to his brother-in-law in Alberta who was producing beef. These regulations made such a transaction impossible. This is one suggestion I make, that the law and the regulations should be amended so that they would not work a hardship on anyone.
Now, returning to my constituency, I would say that when we leave the ranching district we move into the grain producing area. We
Supply-Agriculture
then meet the problems that have been discussed here. Hundreds of words have been said about wheat. I think George Brittnel, a professor at Saskatchewan, wrote p book on wheat, called "More about Wheat". Perhaps if everyone read it there would not be so many words said about wheat. I should like to say, when dealing with the wheat farmer, that the main problem is moving the surplus wheat from the farm to the markets themselves. It does not matter how you pay out the subsidies. After all, the most important thing is to be able to market the commodity at reasonable prices.
I think I have the honour of representing the district in which the two master farmers of Alberta reside. This part of the Bow River constituency is a great wheat producing area. One of the big problems is to get the grain off the farm into the market. One of the problems the farmers have met in this connection is the distribution of box cars. This particular government set up a commission to investigate the distribution of box cars. I have always been amazed by the fact that one of the largest crops western Canada produced in 1928-there were only two other crops to compete with that record-which was between 500 million and 600 million bushels, was transported to market without too much difficulty. There seemed to be plenty of box cars in 1928 to take the whole crop. It seems to me that today there is some aspect of this problem which we have been overlooking. Surely there is sufficient railway equipment today to enable us to get all the wheat off the farms quicker than we have been doing in the past few years.
If these large farmers could get their wheat to market, even if they could fill their quotas on time, then they would have the necessary capital with which to finance their farm operations. I feel that whatever findings this commission makes, the distribution of box cars is a very important item and that is why I have mentioned it. The supply of box cars to the country sidings should be speeded up.
I have heard a lot of members say a lot of things about agriculture, but it does seem to me that the crux of the whole problem can be set forth in a simple formula. How much will a bushel of wheat or a pound of beef buy? One of the big problems today is the cost of production. I wrote one of the farmers in the Bow River constituency for a list of the equipment which he has on the

Supply-Agriculture
farm. He is farming 1,500 acres of land and he has equipment which was purchased anywhere from 1947 up to the present. He uses all this equipment because he is a very efficient farmer; he is one of the master farmers in Alberta. The cost of the equipment he has, based on the cost price at the time of purchase, amounts to $37,493.40. If he went to the market today to buy that same equipment it would cost him $57,500. This illustrates one of the problems. If you consider the cost of that equipment at 1953 prices you will find the cost would be about $30,000, whereas in 1958 the cost would jump to $57,000. The cost of farm machinery has almost doubled, and this seems to be one of the problems.
When I was in the library this morning I was interested in looking back over the records and found that a commission was set up by this house in 1937 to inquire into the price of farm machinery. It may be that the time has arrived when this situation should be reviewed. The cost of farm machinery in Canada seems to be out of all proportion. I want to show hon. members, especially those who do not come from western Canada, how the cost of some of these machines has increased. I am one of those who believe that when the farmer is prosperous the whole economy of the country is in a healthy state. I am not one of those people who play one section of the country against the other section, as has been done by some political parties.
As an example let us consider a 14-foot combine. In 1953 it cost $5,750 and today it would cost $9,800. Then, take a swather; in 1953 it cost $948 and today it will cost $1,149, an increase of about $200. I think one of the most startling examples is that of a Caterpillar D-4 diesel bulldozer with a hydraulic lift. It cost about $5,000 in 1940 and today it costs $15,000. These are just typical examples of the increased cost of farm equipment. It seems to me the time has arrived when we should review the prices of farm machinery in order to keep agriculture in a healthy condition. I should like to know, as a member of parliament, how many dollars worth of labour goes into the construction of this Caterpillar D-4. I should like to know how many dollars of profit result from the sale of this item. The cost of this item would have to be worked right back to the cost of the steel. However, I think that could be done and it is time such an investigation by a new commission was undertaken. We need to know the reason for such increases in farm machinery.
There is one other thing I should mention. I believe the purchasers of farm machinery
[Mr. Woolliams.l
should keep in mind the fact that there is no tariff on farm machinery entering Canada. I ascertained this fact today. This means that a combine has no duty imposed on it. There is no duty imposed on farm machinery entering Canada from the United States. I discussed this question with a member of the customs branch, and he was kind enough to review the list of items I gave him. He said that there were no duties imposed on the list of machines, except two of them. I refer to the list of equipment used on the 1,500-acre farm in Alberta. I have heard many times from political platforms references to the tariff protection given farm machinery, but that just does not exist.
There is one thing about which I am not sure, and I should like to hear an answer to this question if it can be answered. Why does the machinery in the United States cost less? Why does it cost more when it comes into Canada and yet there is no duty imposed upon it? I have heard no answer to this question as yet. I should like, with the permission of the house, to put on Hansard the list of machinery to which I have referred. This shows the list of equiment used on the 1,500-acre farm and also the prices of that equipment in 1953. There are two pages, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: R.C.M.P. REINFORCEMENTS, NFLD.-PROTESTS OVER FEDERAL ACTION
speechtext:
We have heard some discussion today about wheat farmers, both in western Canada and in Ontario. I think the western wheat farmer, like the farmer in any other part of Canada, is a realist and I do not think his opinions can be changed by a drink of liquor. If they were so entertained by some members of the Conservative party as has been said I do not think it is the business of any of the rest of us.
I have every sympathy for the western farmer, as I have for farmers in all other parts of Canada and certainly unless he is farming on a large scale with modern machinery he is facing considerable difficulties at the present time. After listening to the previous speaker this afternoon I have all the greater sympathy with him, because the hon. member for Bow River has brought home to us the high prices which must be paid for implements and machinery.
I do not intend, however, to discuss western farming. I want to refer to a special type of farming in the Niagara district. I want to refer to fruit farming in Ontario and, more particularly, to peaches. The peach crop in 1958 exceeded the peach crop of 1957 by about 15 per cent. The annual meeting of the Ontario peach growers marketing board was held about eight weeks ago at Grimsby and the secretary of that board reported that last year's peach crop was good and that it had exceeded the 1957 crop by something like 15 per cent. Purchases of peaches by processors in 1958 amounted, however, only to 27,444 tons compared with 30,027 tons in 1957. This was a decrease of 10 per cent. The total value of the crop amounted to $2,227,000, and when one includes the $13 a ton paid by the government under the stabilization plan, this amounts to $605,000 less than in 1957. And even with this $13
[Mr. WoolUams.J
taken into account the price obtained for peaches last year was the lowest obtained in years. The same applied to asparagus.
Now previous to 1957 the asparagus crop had been at 23 to 22 cents per pound. In 1957 it fell to 22 cents and 21J cents. When this government came into power I think they set a deficiency payment of three cents below the 18 cent floor price and the farmers never got any more than 15 cents from the processor after that. They got the 15 cents plus the three cents.
In 1958, the number of peach growers selling to processors in the Niagara district declined by nearly 12J per cent, from 1,362 in 1957 to 1,195 in 1958. One reason, of course, was the high cost of production and the low price received for peaches. Another reason this year was the closing down of processing plants. Some of these plants were bought out by United States interests and were not opened. In some cases it was not known whether or not these plants would open, and unless peach producers had made other arrangements for selling their crops, in cases where the plants did not open they could not get rid of them and the peaches rotted on the trees.
I think our two governments should cooperate in helping the fruit farmers to build processing plants. The money would not be lost; it could be amortized over a number of years and the fruit and vegetable farmers would be able to sell their products. Moreover, the money would be spent in Canada and avoid the importation of a lot of fruit from the United States and some other countries, fruit which, I think, is of an inferior quality. What I have said with regard to peaches applies in varying degrees to other fruits and to some vegetables. These processing plants could be used for other fruits and for some vegetables, apart from peaches.
I believe that the main problem which faces the farmer is the obtaining of long and short term credit. This applies to vegetable and fruit farmers as well as to farmers in Ontario generally. The fruit and vegetable growers need short term credit for fertilizer spraying, baskets and so on. At the present time they must pay at least 6 per cent for their money. They also need long term credit for the erection of storage facilities, packing sheds and other buildings. And I am sure they would appreciate it if this government would provide them with processing plants. I am sure this money would be returned. I realize that interest rates must be reasonable and that the Minister of Agriculture should see that they are reasonable.

I fail to see, however, that this government could provide any reasonable rates at the present time because, as you know, in the last two loans made the cost yield to the government was around 5 per cent. In fact, one of the loans was over 5 per cent, and when you take into account income tax gimmicks in connection with those loans they were up around 6J per cent. Therefore, I do not see how the government can lend money to farmers at a very reasonable rate when the net cost of money to them was around 6J per cent. I would hate to think that my credit had fallen so low that I had to pay as much interest as the Minister of Finance had in that last loan. I would appeal to the minister to help our farmers by way of a more reasonable interest rate in order that they might get adequate financing in this highly competitive field of farming.
I must say one thing to the minister. I am sure the fruit and vegetable growers appreciate the longer application of specific duties during the harvest period of the various crops. I do not know how this will apply in the Niagara district, whether it will tend in itself to keep these processing plants open. If it does not I would appeal to this government to do something along with the provincial government of Ontario for the fruit growers.
I also want to say something about the grades of fruit. Our processors have bought grade A fruit from different fruit growers in the past, but when the processors have imported fruit they have accepted a lower grade at a lower price. I think inferior grades have been getting in across the border. Our inspectors let them in. It does not happen any more now than it did with the former government, but it is happening, and I would appeal to the Minister of Agriculture to see that the people in the department at the border admitting fruit and vegetables see that they come up to a definite grade set by our own producers here in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to be able to take part in this debate. I would like first to reply to the statement made by the leader of the C.C.F. party to the effect that the Conservative members of western Canada had betrayed the farmers of western Canada. I believe that the greatest betrayal of the farmers took place in 1946 when the British wheat agreement was signed. According to a statement made by Senator T. A. Crerar in 1953 at a Liberal meeting in Winnipeg, the western farmers had lost at that time over $500 million. In 1946 Mr. Coldwell, the then leader of the C.C.F. party, stated he had given some approval to the British wheat
Supply-Agriculture
agreement. There was nothing wrong with that agreement because it was made in order to help Great Britain, who had made great sacrifices during the war; but where the betrayal came in was that the gift made in the name of Canada was paid for by the farmers of the three western provinces.
When the farmers came to Ottawa last month some of them came to my office, those who came from my constituency of St. Boniface. I told them that their brief had not the proper background, that it had not a proper basis for the demands made. I said that I agreed they had demands to make and that they were not coming here as beggars. I said, "This country owes you at least $500 million." Why was that not mentioned in the brief? The Hon. J. A. MacKinnon, the then minister of trade and commerce, consulted with the western heads of the pools and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in regard to this agreement and they gave it some approval, although the then minister of trade and commerce admitted they had not been consulted as to quantity and price. So this was not a farmers' deal, it was a government deal.
The agreement was signed on July 24, 1946 and it was announced to parliament on the next day, July 25, 1946. It was then a fait accompli, but at that time the then leader of the Conservative party, Mr. John Bracken, and the late Mr. Arthur Ross of Souris, took a definite stand against that deal. They stated it was not fair to the farmers, and that if the farmers were going to sell their grain at 50 cents less than what it was worth in the world market they should be given parity prices.

Mr. Chairman, when you
called it six o'clock I was talking about the great betrayal of the western wheat growers by the Liberal and C.C.F. parties in 1946. As I said before the adjournment, in 1953, as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of January 24 of that year, Senator Crerar was reported to have stated that the grain growers of western Canada had lost $500 million under the British wheat agreement and the international wheat agreement.

When the delegation from St. Boniface came to my office I spoke to them about that and they urged me to mention it at the first opportunity and that is why I am raising this question tonight. When the delegation appeared before the committee on agriculture I referred to that point as well. Mr. Harry Marsh of Saskatchewan who had at one time been a director of the wheat pool agreed that if the march had taken place in 1946 it would have been possible for the farmers to obtain at that time what they are seeking now.
I am really surprised that the farmers did not march on Ottawa in 1946 when the Liberal party of that day without any authority and without consultation with the western farmers confiscated part of their income from wheat. It was really a conscription of wealth directed only against the three western provinces.
This afternoon I heard the leader of the C.C.F. party talking about the interests of the western farmers being betrayed by the policies of the Conservative party but the greatest betrayal occurred in 1946 at which time the C.C.F. and Liberal parties worked hand in hand. Mr. Coldwell admitted that he had given some approval to that agreement at that time.
It seems to me that hon. members of the C.C.F. were not concerned at all about the interests of the western farmer. They were concerned only in bringing about an enforced plan and fixed prices and government interference with the affairs of the western farmer. They did not consider what losses the western farmers were taking at that time.
I am surprised that Mr. Wesson, who I understand was also a leader of the wheat pool in 1946, did not look after the interests of the farmers then. Perhaps the organized march on Ottawa was caused by remorse or perhaps he is now repentant for what he did to the farmers in 1946. I am quite surprised that the leader of the C.C.F. party at this time is not interested in asking any questions about the British wheat agreement or about the stand that party took at that time.

Yes, indeed. I would invite him to explain the participation of his party in that agreement and tell the committee why they did not try to lead a march on Ottawa at that time when one was required. At that time there was no farmers' union organized in western Canada. Indeed, the very reason for the organization of the farmers' union in the western provinces was that the interests of the farmers were not being properly looked after by the C.C.F. or by the wheat pool organization. The farmers saw the necessity of having another organization and thus established the farmers' union. Personally I am

sorry they were not organized before they were. If that had been done what took place in 1946 could have been prevented. Such a thing has never happened to any other class in Canada. No other group has had part of the income from its produce confiscated and given away to another country with the cost of the gift being charged only to one class, namely the wheat growers of the three prairie provinces.
The province of Ontario was exempted. In some years that province has grown as much wheat as the province of Manitoba. Why was not the province of Ontario included? Obviously they knew they could not get away with it for political reasons and therefore it was limited to the three prairies provinces and to only one class. I believe this represented a mortal blow struck at the western farmer. In the course of a few years $500 million was taken away from them. I have taken this figure from Honourable T. A. Crerar who was a member of the Liberal cabinet at one time but who did not approve of it after he ceased to be in the cabinet. He said so in Winnipeg on January 24, 1953, at a Liberal convention, of all places.
In 1946 that great newspaper of western Canada, the Winnipeg Free Press, put up a wonderful fight against the policy of the Liberal party at that time and in defence of the interests of the three western provinces.
I was quite shocked last week when I heard the hon. member for Essex East expressing concern for what was happening at this time to the western farmer. Why did he not show equal concern when his administration was in office at which time he had some authority and power to protect the wheat growers of western Canada?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to place on record the position of the Conservative party in 1946 by quoting some remarks made in this house by the then leader of the Conservative party, Mr. John Bracken. This is to be found at page 4822 of Hansard of August 15, 1946. Mr. John Bracken, made the following comments regarding the British wheat agreement:
It is a bad agreement because it proposes to sell 160 million bushels of wheat to Britain at 50 cents a bushel below the world price. It is either a gift or it is an improvident trade arrangement. If it is a gift, let us say so. But if it is supposed to be an insurance against low prices in the future-if because we take less for our wheat today than it is worth Britain is expected to pay more for our wheat two years from now than the world price when it may be lower, I say that as an insurance that this will be done, it is valueless.
It is a bad bargain also because it will create friction between Britain and Canada. If in two or three years from now the world price of wheat is low and Britain does not come through with a higher price to us than the world price then is, we shall feel that she has reneged on this agreement. On the other hand, if two or three years from now, when the world price of wheat may be low, we press Britain to pay us more than the world price, she will feel that we are unreasonable. So I say that the proposal is altogether likely to create friction between this country and Britain.
The third reason why this is a bad bargain is that it will cause friction with other nations as well. It will invite criticism from the wheat-producing nations, because here we are selling wheat to the greatest wheat importer of the world at 50 cents a bushel below the world price. What are other wheat-producing nations to think of a policy of that kind?
At page 4824 of Hansard of the same date Mr. Bracken said:
Now with respect to the government's wheat policy generally. I make this criticism: it is not fair to the farmers, it is not fair to a quarter of the Canadian people, it is not fair-particularly- to those who are growing wheat. It is not fair because of the price that is offered, $1.35, while there is a possibility that something more will be coming after the end of five years, there is no assurance that there will be. One dollar and thirty-five cents is not a fair price for wheat today. It is not a "parity price", if I may use that hackneyed term. "Parity price" is the name given to a price which is supposed to express a fair price in relation to other things. The parity price now would be about $1.53, but $1.35 is all the farmers are assured, at a time when the world price is nearly half as high again as that. If the farmers of Canada cannot be assured of a parity price now, when the world price is high, what prospect is there of their being assured of parity price when the world price is low, as it is sure to be later on?
If I may stop here, I think Mr. John Bracken gave a real good picture of what was going to happen. I would like to know
Supply-Agriculture
where the C.C.F. party was at that time when the Conservative leader was talking about parity price? I continue to quote:
The government's policy during the last two or three years has been a policy generally of floors and ceilings. That has reduced the wide fluctuations of prices, and to that extent is good; it has raised the floors and lowered the ceilings. Now there is a modification of that policy. The government comes along with this price of $1.35, which as I have said is less than parity. The policy has been one of floors and ceilings, but now it is one even more of a controlled economy; and when the government starts in to control the economy, then when things do not go right, or any inequity is brought about, the government has no one to blame but itself. This policy is not equitable. It does not assure equity to farmers, and this is one time when the government might have given them that assurance.
As I have said, the government's policy is one of no assurance of parity when the world price is high, and even less assurance when the world price is low. The government's policy is one of making agriculture carry the cost of the loss on this sale. It is not the nation that is carrying it. The nation's economy will suffer if it does not get as much for wheat as it might have got. But the price of the loss will be borne by the farmers. The government may say that the farmers are probably getting enough, but the fact is that this is a contribution by the farmers of Canada and not by the Canadian people as a whole. When you stop to think that on this one commodity the crop is sold at four different prices-wheat for flour at 78 cents, the so-called domestic price of $1.25, the British price of $1.55, and now the effort is being made to sell to other countries at over $2-you will realize that is very much of a hodge-podge, something which is most difficult to administer and does not work out equitably to the producers.
In Hansard for that year hon. members can also read the very good speech of the late member for Souris, Arthur Ross and the good speech of the present Prime Minister against this agreement. I believe I have performed the duty requested of me by the delegates who came from the constituency of St. Boniface by bringing this matter to the attention of the committee. Thank you.

Regardless of what happens in the next election, whether one member present in the house tonight or present in this government or in this parliament is returned at the next election, I think they can all say, with the exception of one and that one is the hon. member for Assiniboia, that this government has been more sympathetic to western

I think they can all say that never has a more united effort been put forth on behalf of the western farmers than has been put forth by the members of this government and of this party during the last session and up to date.
I just wonder how sincere this member from western Canada, the hon. member for Assiniboia, this preacher of doom, despair and destruction, has been in his support of the western farmer? How sincere are his colleagues in the group of eight, how sympathetic are they to the western farmers? I just want to read one short excerpt from Hansard of last year containing words uttered by a voice of the party that he represents. It is to be found on page 3509 of Hansard for August 14, 1958 and reads as follows:
This does not concern resources about which we know nothing. This relates to the breadbasket of this country, and I suggest to the minister that the breadbasket of this country is no longer on the prairies; it is in the boreal forests where we find our pulp and paper resources.
Then there was an interjection by an hon. member who said:
What does the hon. member for Assiniboia say to that?
Then the hon. member whom I am quoting went on:
He has just been complaining from behind. I do not mind somewhat overstating this point in relation to what the hon. member for Assiniboia tells me. but I think we have gone on long enough paying such marked attention to the agricultural interests especially to the grain interests.
What solution has the hon. member for Assiniboia put forth on behalf of the farmers? How does he propose to assist farming? How well has he briefed his group of eight? Without referring to Hansard I remember that last year one of his colleagues was speaking on agriculture and asked the western members who had been fighting for the western farmers why we could not solve our problem in the same way that labour solves theirs. He said that when labour encounters an increase in the cost of living all they do is go to the employer and make an arrangement with the employer whereby he raises their salaries. How can the western farmer go to his buyer and say, "My cost of living is going up; I want more money for my grain".
I also suggest that the hon. member for Assiniboia should brief the spokesmen for his party when he has duties elsewhere as to what the problems of the western farmers are. I suggest that by the tactics he has been following during this session-not so much during last session-he is doing every-


thing within the power of one man to divide the efforts of the western farmers in obtaining their rights. He professes to be an agrarian. From his numerous speeches we have heard that he is an expert in all fields. He is an expert on external affairs. He is an expert on shipping. He is an expert on labour. He is an expert on finance. In fact, last year when he was criticizing the budget he was asked how he would go about balancing the budget. He said that he would tax the millionaires and multimillionaires and get the money from them. I wonder how long that source would last. I wonder what he would do when it was exhausted. I wonder how long it would be before he got down to the timber barons and I wonder whether there would be seven instead of eight at that time in the little group to your left, Mr. Chairman.
I could say more but I think the remarks I have already made will prove to all Canadians that if he cannot convince that little group of eight he can never hope to convince the people of Canada. What does he hope to gain by his remarks this afternoon, by the co-operation that we as members from the west are getting from him? Is he seeking assistance for the farmers or political gain? I leave it to hon. members to answer that question. I suggest that the people of Canada are not as gullible as the hon. member for Assiniboia believes them to be.
With regard to the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, Mr. Chairman, I have heard it said very often, quite often by the group of eight to your left, that the western farmer is not getting his fair share of the national wealth. The term "fair share of the national wealth" is one of many such terms that they use and the reason they use it is that there are no statistics to prove it. I have written to the dominion bureau of statistics to find out what the fair share of the national wealth is so far as the agrarian is concerned. The bureau does not have such figures on its files and is not able to give them.
However, I have heard the minister say that farmers comprise 12 per cent of our population and that that 12 per cent receive 6 per cent of the national income. I suggest to the minister that there is a problem in western Canada when 12 per cent of the people receive only 6 per cent of the national income. There must be something wrong with either the economy of our country or our mode of living. However, in my view the statement of the minister is not entirely correct because in the west at the present time stockmen are enjoying good returns from their cattle. There are a great number of stockmen on the prairies and this brings up the average.

Our concern as western members, and I think I can speak for all western members of this party, is with the situation of the grain farmer. That is the immediate problem. The problem of the grain farmer is that he purchases everything that he needs on a protected market while all the grain he sells is sold on a competitive market. This results in what is known as the cost price squeeze or high cost of production. Before there is a division between eastern and western farmers I would suggest that the problem of the high cost of production applies to the eastern farmers as well as the western farmers. As farmers let us not be divided on that point. As has happened in the past, let us not have eastern farmers fighting western farmers. Let us not have any member of the house, as we heard this afternoon, try to divide the farmers.
In the past members representing several different parties have been sent to the House of Commons and after what I heard this afternoon I can understand why those representing eastern ridings could not understand the western problem. The western members who were sent here could not even agree among themselves. They did not put forward the problem of the western farmer. They were fighting party politics.
For the benefit of eastern members I wish to point out one thing that has bothered the grain farmers of the west for many years. At the present time the people of Canada are buying wheat 15 to 20 cents a bushel cheaper than it can be purchased anywhere else. Let us suppose all Canadian farmers stopped producing wheat and the Canadian people had to buy wheat for home consumption from some other source. They would pay at least 15 to 20 cents a bushel more than they are paying today. Instead of the income of the western or other grain farmer going up, it has been gradually going down. Today the Canadian people are buying wheat cheaper than any person on the North American continent can buy it. This is not a fair situation in an economy that is rising.
For purposes of clarification I suggest that we divide our economy into three parts. We will call the first group labour, the second group management and the third group the consumers. The reason I call the third group consumers is that our western farmers come within that term. I think what applies to all western farmers applies to all consumers. I include eastern farmers in that group.
Now, which one of these three groups receives the most out of our economy today? All the members are supplied with the literature from the labour organizations. We receive the labour magazines, and I think
Supply-Agriculture
the labour people will admit that within the last 10 years they have increased their net income, over and above the increased cost of living, by 27 per cent. Management, on the other hand, can always look after itself. Whatever it costs management to produce an article, their percentage of profit can always be added to that cost of production and passed along to the consumer.
I would suggest that the consumer group is the only group that has not been protected by legislation. I would suggest that at this session or very soon the government should intervene on behalf of the consumer group. I would suggest also that so far as the farmers who are included in that consumer group are concerned, the minister might give serious consideration to the question of the two price system. I do not think any western member will maintain that the two price system will solve all the problems of western Canada. However, I think we will say that such a system would put western farmers on a firm basis and they would not have to come to the government year after year for assistance.
This two price system has been ignored by certain large farm groups in the west, to which reference was made this afternoon on several occasions. I should like to read a part of an article that was published in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix on April 8, 1959. It was an article about the dean of agriculture in the University of Saskatchewan, Professor Rupert Ramsay. In this article it is stated that Professor Ramsay said the net farm income in Saskatchewan last year was $2,000 per farm. Professor Ramsay said that the prairie farmer had established a case for some kind of additional income. Canadian farmers had difficulty selling in the British market because agricultural prices in the United Kingdom were much lower than in Canada. The only alternative to this problem was to establish a two price system with one price for the domestic market and one for international markets.
Efforts have been made by one member from western Canada, Mr. Chairman, to belittle what other western members have done, particularly in connection with the farmers' march on Ottawa. I want to inform this house that any misunderstanding that has arisen between the marchers and the members from the west has not been in regard to the problems of western Canada. I think we will all agree that there is a serious problem there. Any misunderstanding that arose was in connection with the solution of that problem. They say deficiency payments are the solution, and most of us contend that the two price system would be. The reason we have
2S98

Supply-Agriculture
not supported deficiency payments, as the marchers thought we would and as the hon. member for Assiniboia tried to make out we should, is that while he was elsewhere last year all the western members were here studying the problem. We have studied the problem of deficiency payments and we have come to the conclusion that they will not solve our problem. However, we do believe the two price system will put us well on our way.
I should like to say just a word or two further in regard to the fence-sitting, if you wish to call it that, the hon. member for Assiniboia is doing. He professes now to be the champion of labour. He also professes to be the champion of agriculture, an agrarian. An agrarian is not against tariffs in the east. He is not against good wages for labour. But, when he starts to suffer he must do something. This afternoon the hon. member for Bow River mentioned that there is no tariff on farm machinery. He may be quite correct in his contention, but I wish to point out to him that we know we are paying $150, roughly, per ton for Canadian steel when we could purchase other steel for $100. We do know that the textiles the farmers are using can be purchased for one-third less. When your income starts to get so low you feel that pressure then you are bound to complain and you are bound to look around to try to ascertain the source of that pressure.
I recall that last year there was a strike on the west coast which prevented shipments of our wheat. They say a strike does not hurt anyone. I refer to labour's own words which may be found in a memorandum presented by labour to this government. They say:
We would simply say that compulsory arbitration is prejudicial to the tree play of collective bargaining; it substitutes third party intervention tor settlement by the parties themselves; it is a restriction on the very important civil right to strike.
It would appear from this statement that labour is not too concerned with the civil rights of other groups who also feel the results of any strike action. In a democratic country such as we have I would suggest that civil rights must apply to all persons and not to those of any special class, race or hue. We might well ask, what protection does the third party, the consumers' group receive under the present method of negotiation. I suggest they receive none. I wish the hon. member for Assiniboia would listen to this. Labour also states in their memorandum to the government:
We believe the increased wage earner purchasing power is essential to lift us out of the recession.
How can the hon. member for Assiniboia relate this statement to the declaration of the farm groups who state:

The drop in the purchasing power of the grain farmers was one of the major causes of the present unemployment problem. When farmers lack money to buy goods and services, other Canadians are deprived of their jobs.
How can he sit on the fence? Let him go one way or the other and inform this house which way he is going. He cannot serve two masters.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I want to assure the minister that I shall not try his patience for long; I just want to make a few short remarks on the position of farmers in my riding and in the district of Saguenay-Lake St. John.
While listening to the various speeches this afternoon, I noticed that there were problems, not only in our part of the country but also everywhere else in Canada, which obviously confirm the findings of the final report established by the Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects, as may be seen on page 149, and I quote:
Along the south and southeast coast of Nova Scotia, in much of Cape Breton Island, in the central and northeastern sections of New Brunswick, and in the Gaspe, as well as in Newfoundland, many of the farms are hardly above the subsistence level; and this is also true of northern Quebec and northern Ontario.
We also have many agricultural problems in my riding and throughout our district, Mr. Chairman. There are large families working on farms and, as the children grow up, they are to a certain extent attracted by the urban centres and industries and, little by little, because there is no possibility of finding adequate subsistence on the farm for the whole family, the young people leave the farm and increase the number of those who work in factories and offices in the cities of my riding and district.

This does not necessarily mean that young people dislike agriculture. I am certain that those who are born on the land are in many cases very much attracted by it, but today it seems as if the land had some difficulty in providing a living and certain amenities for those who till the soil. I think that it is not enough that the land should provide mere subsistence to those who work it, but that the young people, and the not so young too, should reap a few amenities when living and working on the farm. This, I think, is one of the main problems which must be faced by the farmers in my riding and in the whole area.
To those problems must be added more recent issues like agricultural mechanization, for instance. There are of course, I admit, the Agricultural Credit Board of Quebec and the Canadian Farm Loan Board who help our farmers and agriculturists, but I believe that at least in the case of the federal body- and conditions were about the same under the former administration-the interest rate is somewhat too high for our farmers. Farmers should be able to borrow money at a lower interest rate.
Farmers-those of my constituency, at least-have complained about the enormous difference there is between the cost of production of agricultural machinery and their sale price. I recall, in particular, a farmer of a rural parish close to Jonquiere who explained to me, for instance, how much a potato seeder would cost. He quoted prices to me on production costs and sale price of such a machine, and I believe that, if these figures were right, the situation is rather alarming, not only in our district, but in the whole country.
The minister or his department should try to investigate the discrepancy between the production cost of farm implements and their selling price to the farmers, because as a result of that discrepancy, the farmer is having a bad time today.
I note, for instance, in L'Action Catholique of March 14, 1958, an article from which I shall quote only one paragraph concerning the capital which the farmers must earmark for their farm machinery. I quote:
Quebec farmers who, from 1941 to 1946, bought a little over 30 million dollars worth of machinery, spent $130 million from 1947 to 1953 to mechanize their farms.
All those problems are being added to the difficulties facing the farmers of my constituency, of the area, and, I believe, of the country as a whole.
We are on the threshold of an era which is not new perhaps-it started some time ago-and I believe the government should en-
Supply-Agriculture
deavour to study the problem in a very special way, in order to come to the rescue of the farmers and develop their interest in their farms. That would avoid, no doubt to a great extent, the exodus to the cities because as farmers move into cities, after working on the farm all their lives, they have no trade nor any specific profession and they have trouble finding jobs. In fact, they are taken as temporary employees in industry, in office work or public buildings, and as soon as that temporary work is over, they go and swell the ranks of the unemployed in the larger centres of the country.
I think the government should look into this problem and try to do something in this field.
At the beginning of my remarks, I told the minister that I would not exercise his patience to any great length, but I should like to close my remarks with a quotation, from the final report of the Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects, dealing with economic conditions affecting Canada's farmers. I quote:
Governments, however, will have a role to play in hastening and facilitating changes that would in any case be brought about by economic forces, and in tempering the winds of change so that individual farmers do not feel too fleeced and forgotten. There will thus be need for government assistance in agriculture over the next 25 years; but the assistance will probably take different forms than in the past.
That is why I have no hesitation in saying that the government should have an aggressive policy in the agricultural field. Gone are the days when grants were made to assist people in clearing their own land, or in building a small house as shelter for the father, mother and two or^ three children. This is a new era, and in my view, the government should begin to realize the implications of this new era which started not so long ago, and should try to do something to keep farmers on the land.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few brief comments I would like to make on item 1 of the agricultural estimates, and those comments will relate to the administration of the Agricultural Stabilization Act. First of all, I would like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture and the members of the staff in his department for the good job they have made of this administration over the past year. All members in this house will recognize that the task of the minister and his officials has been a very difficult one.

There has been much talk and many exhortations from different quarters about holding the price line in our economy. The price line during the last fiscal year has not been held too well, and for that reason I would urge upon the minister and the government the necessity of holding the stabilization price line as it affects farm commodities. We had many instances during the last year of increases being granted in wages in our industries, and in transportation particularly. The other day we completed voting a grant of $20 million to subsidize freight rates so that higher wages could be paid those in the transport field. It is very important that farm prices should not be allowed to drop.
It was one of the undertakings of the party now responsible for our government, an undertaking made both during the last election and before, that they would do their utmost to see that the agricultural interests of this country received a fairer share of the national income. For that reason it is necessary now, to do everything possible to hold the stabilization price line.
Everyone will appreciate the statement of the minister today in connection with dairy products. This has been a very pressing problem. The method of stabilization has not given exactly the results that were desired in the dairy industry. Far-reaching changes have been made and other changes are promised for the future. I do not know whether the over-all results will have the effect of holding the stabilization price line in the dairy industry but I am sure it is the sincere desire of all interested hon. members that this new method will maintain or increase the over-all support.
In connection with soybeans that are grown extensively in the constituency which I represent and in the constituencies to the south and west of it, representations have been made to the government recently requesting that soybeans again be designated a commodity under the Agricultural Stabilization Act and that the price be stabilized for the 1959 crop. I hope it will be possible for the minister and the government to again hold the stabilization price line in relation to soybeans.
We do not grow half enough soybeans in Canada to supply our own requirements. It is felt that if an incentive price could be placed on soybeans it would take acreage out of the production of some other crops such
Supply-Agriculture
as wheat which are in surplus supply. Not only would the incentive to grow more soybeans have that effect but it would save us up to $15 million or $20 million a year that is spent for the importation of soybeans.
The same conditions apply to sugar beets. We grow but a small percentage of the sugar which we consume in Canada. From the point of view of the creation of jobs as well as from the point of view of conserving our exchange and keeping our money within our own country and promoting our own industry we should increase our production of sugar beets and beet sugar. The sugar beet growers have also requested that sugar beets again be supported for the 1959 crop. I am sure it is the hope of all concerned that the government will be able to hold the stabilization price line in regard to sugar beets or even increase the support price.
Some sections of our canning industry are complaining that imports of canned fruits and vegetables are creating extremely stiff competition within Canada for the canning industries located here. It is to be hoped that the committee which the Minister of Agriculture has set up to inquire into the whole canning industry in Canada will be able to ascertain whether or not the economic climate that now surrounds the canning industry is such as to encourage that industry to expand, at least to the point where it will supply our domestic requirements.
The Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act is only one feature of the over-all program which this government has devised for the creation of better conditions for the Canadian agricultural industry. The farmers themselves can do much to assist in the solution of their economic problems by organizing themselves more closely and efficiently under the farm products marketing acts which have been set up in most of our provinces. If they will take that action, organize themselves effectively and adopt the necessary measures to bring their production into line with our national requirements, it would go a long way toward solving our agricultural problems. It is my opinion-and I offer this as a suggestion to the minister and the government-that the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act should be used in every way possible, not only to stabilize agriculture temporarily but also to encourage farmers to so organize and control their own production and their own destiny.

Mr. Chairman, we have already had five days of discussion on the first item of the agricultural estimates and I do not propose to take much more of the time of the committee in making my contribution. In any event I certainly do not intend to deliver a diatribe such as was thrown at us this afternoon by the C.C.F. member who represents the constituency of Skeena and who, although a labour man from the Pacific coast, is now apparently one of that party's experts on the problems of western farmers.
I do, however, wish to make a brief comment concerning one or two matters. First of all I should like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture for the great planning that must have taken place in the preparation of these estimates now before us. It has been brought out before but I should like to emphasize again that the minister in his estimates has expenditures of $106,079,852 for this year, expenditures all of direct benefit to our great industry of agriculture. According to page 2 of the estimate book, the estimates for the Department of Agriculture are the sixth highest of all departmental estimates. I believe this indicates very forcibly the great interest this government has in the welfare of farmers all across Canada.
I hold in my hand a very interesting statement on the farm situation, Mr. Chairman. It is a statement by the Leader of the Opposition which I think should be put on the record because it puts the farm problem in its proper perspective. The little pamphlet is entitled: "Statements from the Hon. L. B. Pearson, September-November, 1958, as Reported in the Daily Newspapers". It was circulated and apparently a copy was given to me.
According to a statement in the Edmonton Journal of October 3, 1958, as reported in the publicity from the Liberal party headquarters, the Liberal leader said:
It is clear that agriculture has not had a fair share of the national income for the past 10 or 15 years.
It goes on to say:
The government in power at the present time "has a duty to do something about that".
In other words, Mr. Chairman, the Liberal leader says that the former government did not help the farmers and this government should do something about it. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this government is doing something about it. Other speakers have

given an outline of the long list of things that this government has already done in our long range farm program. Other parts of the program will be introduced in the house in the next few weeks.
While out in Moose Jaw-Lake Centre during the Easter recess I noted press reports implying that western members on the government side were not friendly to the mass delegation. In fact, it was suggested that we were not working in the interests of western agriculture. That is not true, Mr. Chairman. Most of the western government members are farmers themselves, or are directly connected with prairie agriculture. The 47 members from the three prairie provinces realize that we represent the western farmers, as we also represent business and professional groups and labour in our various constituencies. I think we did everything we possibly could to help in the visit of the mass delegation to Ottawa.
This does not mean that all of us agreed with the demands of that mass delegation for deficiency payments. I am not convinced myself that deficiency payments on the wheat, oats and barley delivered in the last three crop years is the most equitable way of distributing any help that this government may see fit to give. I am in the same position as the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose who spoke earlier. If the government gave deficiency payments in the manner suggested in the mass delegation brief on the amount of grain delivered to the elevators in the last three crop years I, too, would receive most of the maximum payment of $4,500 suggested in the brief as the limit to any individual farmer. I know many farmers in Moose Jaw-Lake Centre who would receive only a few hundred dollars by this suggested plan of cash distribution, and I imagine that their needs for cash are as great as mine, or as great as the needs of other farmers who, too, would receive the $4,500 maximum payment.
The problems of agriculture have occupied more of our time at this session than any other problem in Canada. I have stated this before and I certainly believe it. The standing committee on agriculture, of which I am a member, already has had several meetings, and we certainly will have many more meetings as other parts of the government's long range farm program are presented.
The question of the average cost of production for prairie grain farmers has been

brought up on many occasions. It is realized that such a cost of production figure is necessary before a definite relationship between farm income and farm expenses can be established.
As an example of how farm costs may vary, I have two recent statements from farmers in the northern section of my own constituency of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. The one farmer from around Watrous has just over 1,000 cultivated acres. His statement shows that in 1955, the first year in which deficiency payments are sought from the government, his total farm receipts-and these are his figures-were $14,873.39; but according to his figures his total operating costs were $17,176.47, without allowing, as he says, for any interest on his investment or any wages for himself. The farm, he says, is strictly a grain farm. Therefore, it fits into the picture of most of the farmers who came down on the delegation. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, in 1955, his total farm receipts were $14,873.39 and his operating costs were $17,176.47. This grain farmer shows in his statement a net loss of $2,302.67. These are his exact figures as he gave them to me, down to the last cent.
In 1956, the second year of demand for deficiency payments, he shows total receipts of $21,082.70 from his farm, and total operating cost of $18,035.73, for a net income this time of $3,056.97.
In 1957, the third year of deficiency payments claimed, his total receipts are shown as $13,748.54 and total operating costs as $16,330.09, or a net loss of $2,591.55.
In 1958, his total receipts were $11,069 and his total operating costs $14,332.12, or a net loss of $3,262.43. This actual statement was presented to me, Mr. Chairman, as an argument for deficiency payments.
For the benefit of the western members who are practical farmers, I will repeat the operating costs as given on this strictly grain farm of 1,050 cultivated acres. His costs include depreciation on machinery but, as he says, make no allowance for interest on his investment or payment of wages to himself. In 1955, total operating costs were $17,176.47; in 1956, $18,035.73; in 1957, $16,330.09; in 1958, $14,332.12. As I say, the farmer states these figures do not include any interest on his investment or any wages to himself.
I make no comment on these operating figures, Mr. Chairman. I myself think they are very high for an efficient grain farmer, but I just put them on the record for the consideration of the committee.
In contrast to this statement for deficiency payments, I have another letter from a farmer

near Govan. This letter has been referred to in the house before, I shall read just one brief excerpt from the letter. This farmer writes:
I am a farmer, farming one section of average land, have no other enterprise but grain growing, so work at my occupation only about six months of the year. Have gathered assets to the value of approximately $60,000 in 18 years and still would be eligible for most of the proposed deficiency payments.

This second letter includes a year by year statement which shows that in 1942 the farmer was a renter on a half section, with no equity in the land he was working. Now, by his own statement, he has clear title to a section of land, has nearly $10,000 worth of machinery, no livestock and 12,000 bushels of grain in store on his farm on December 31, 1958.
I mention these two statements given to me by grain farmers in my own constituency to emphasize the problem of arriving at an average cost of production figure that could have some application for all prairie grain farms. The grain farmer who reported he has had total receipts of $70,774.72 in the past four farming years asks for deficiency payments. The other grain farmer, who has paid for a section of land since 1940, writes in his letter:
I am of the firm opinion that any farmer operating a section or more of land reasonably efficiently should be in no need of assistance of any kind, excepting crop failure.
I quote these two statements, Mr. Chairman, to illustrate the great divergence in the views of western farmers themselves. I realize that the Department of Trade and Commerce, through the dominion bureau of statistics, is attempting to arrive at a fair figure for an average farm cost of production. I suggest that until we can obtain some such figure we cannot properly solve the farm problem. I think the example of the costs of the two farmers, as given by themselves, proves the need for some fair average figure.
I hope the Minister of Agriculture can help to impress on the bureau of statistics the necessity of quick action in this regard to obtain a fairly accurate cost of production figure. Again, Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture on the manner in which he is running his department. Mr. Chairman, I rise at this point of the debate, not as an expert in agriculture, but rather as the representative of a mostly rural constituency. I would like to congratulate the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) because, when he took on his duties, he was faced with a national agricultural situation that was particularly difficult, and even if, today, everything is not yet perfect, we must admit that the new leadership he has given to the government's farming policy augurs well for the farmer.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to launch into elaborate remarks about agriculture; I intend simply to express a few general ideas and a few proposals about problems pertaining to my constituency. Dairying is the chief agricultural industry in my constituency. So, today it was with great satisfaction, that I learned, as did all hon. members, that the price of butter had just been fixed at 64 cents a pound. It is good news for the farmers of my constituency and they will surely rejoice and congratulate the government for it. My colleague, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard), has emphasized earlier certain problems which affect the agricultural industry of the province of Quebec, and particularly, the problem of the diseases which often cripple our herds. I can only endorse his remarks and ask, as he did, that the government increase its help programs aimed at protecting dairy herds.
There is also another problem which was emphasized the other day by our colleagues the hon. members for Bellechasse and Charlevoix (Messrs. Dorion and Asselin) a problem which also concerns the farmers of my riding, and that is the pulpwood problem. Those two hon. members have outlined the wrongs done to farmers who were cutting pulpwood on their farms. I can only approve what they said and ask that the necessary arrangements be made so that farmers be favoured in this field as well as in the others.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) referred in a general way to problems which particularly affect farmers. He emphasized in particular the exodus from the farm. It must be said that in our area, just as in many other communities, there is massive desertion of the farms. Different reasons account for this, but they can be related in many cases to the difficulties laid in the path of young men who would like to continue working on the farm. The situation of those young farmers is untenable on account of the very high cost of production which the farmers of the different areas of Canada must meet. The
[Mr. Pascoe.l
situation causes uneasiness and financial hardship which compel or incite farmers' sons to leave the farm and move to the cities to work in factories.
Mr. Chairman, that situation would certainly not be so bad if, during the last 20 or 22 years, the government had given the same attention to the farm industry as it did to other industrial sectors. Because the interest shown to the farm industry was not as great as that shown to the substantial industrialization which developed throughout Canada during the period I just mentioned, we now see that desertion turn into uneasiness and a most alarming calamity.
Mr. Chairman, mention was made a moment ago of another problem facing the farmers who want to earn their living on a farm, and that is the problem of mechanization; that problem is important because the cost of farm implements which the farmers must purchase if they want to operate their farm according to modern techniques is so high that they cannot meet the excessive price of the farm equipment they have to buy. Again in that field, there is plenty of food for thought; research should be made by the various governments in order to help the farmers meet the requirements of mechanized operation.
In conclusion, I would like to make a suggestion for the benefit of my constituency. My riding of Roberval is known throughout the province of Quebec, and I hope throughout Canada also, as the blueberry riding. It is, moreover, partly to this that we owe the name usually given to us. According to statistics supplied to me by the experimental farm of Normandin, between 1942 and 1956, about 14,220,000 pounds of blueberries were gathered each year representing an annual value of $1,961,641. You can appreciate that this is an extremely important income on which the farmers of my riding have come to rely. It is an important item because it is usually a net income since farmers are able to engage in this extremely profitable occupation at little cost.
During the past years, following research made at the Normandin experimental farm, it was found that the blueberry industry could be one of the most profitable industries for the riding of Roberval and the neighbouring area. But the development of this industry depends on certain research, on certain soil conditions, on soil analysis and on the reclamation of those lands known as "blueberry lands".
That is why, as was stated some time ago by the superintendent of the federal experimental farm in Normandin, the federal government should consider the possibility of setting up, at the experimental station

in Normandin, a sub-station to study and analyse the reclamation methods of those blueberry lands, to study the "control" of vegetation which has nothing to do with blueberries, and to look after the "control" of the diseases and insects which threaten blueberry production.
I make this suggestion to the Minister of Agriculture Mr. Chairman, because the farmers in my riding, since my election, have been urging me to to ask the Department of Agriculture to deal especially with this problem. As I mentioned a while ago, this is an important industry bringing as it does to the farmers in my riding a supplementary income which is, at least as far as I know, for a great number of them a convenient way to make both ends meet.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take up the time of the house any longer. I will have an opportunity to take up this matter again at a later stage when we consider the agricultural estimates. I shall then try to establish a case for some agricultural issues which affect the province of Quebec as a whole as well as the riding I represent in this house.

Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure for me even at this late hour to take part in this debate on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture and to draw to the attention of the minister and the house some problems my fellow-citizens of Nickel Belt asked me to submit for their consideration.
I speak especially on behalf of my fellow-citizens who live in the French river area, the valley of Noeville, St. Charles and Alban, as well as the Warren area, Blezard Valley, Chelmsford, the heart of this riding, famous for its potatoes.
Notwithstanding this late hour, I would like to make a few remarks on the problems facing the average farmer in this country. Practically all day, we have heard representations mostly from western members. I agree heartily that the problems they are trying to solve are most important. But I would not like, on account of the serious problems confronting wheat growing in their provinces, to see a lack of interest for the problems facing the average farmer in northern Ontario and northern Quebec.
A while ago, the member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) brought to the attention of this house, and I agree with his remark, that the report on the economic prospects of Canada makes it clear in particular that the farm problems confronting northern Quebec and northern Ontario are probably as serious as in the west.
The people engaged in agriculture in my constituency are average farmers who in
Supply-Agriculture
fact own but some 80 acres of land. We have noticed, since this government came to power, that our farmers are faced with many problems and I would like to bring to the attention of this house that these troubles are probably due to the promises which were made to the farmers before the last election. In fact, the promise was given, and emphatically, that the Conservative government, if re-elected, would give Canadian farmers a greater share of the national income. After the election, the farmer was therefore justified in believing that the government would bring in the remedies it had mentioned.
But after some amendments were introduced last year to farm legislation farmers increased their production and hardly a year later, we realize that the problems facing us in agriculture as well as in other fields have grown worse.
Today, Mr. Chairman, the minister's statement in the house showed that the direction given by him to agriculture gave rise to certain problems. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) was hardly less than ridiculous, a moment ago, when he said that, according to him, the minister's statement this afternoon indicated that special attention had been given to powdered milk production. But if we look over the minister's statement, we find that he wished rather to stop the assistance given that industry. It is so true that on the last page of his statement, he states that the established price will be granted only in part, until September of this year and stopped completely at that date.
That is why I say that the government is responsible for the crisis in that field. In fact, we read on the first page of the minister's statement that over-production of powdered milk was 103 million pounds, since the total production was 187 million pounds. This is to say that over-production in this country was, in a proportion of over 60 per cent, the result of the department's action.
In the light of those figures, I trust the minister will try, in the future, to avoid creating such a serious problem.
Mr. Chairman, there may be a point which affects more particularly the people in my district and I am speaking of farm financing. Several times last year in this house and at least on one occasion this year, we discussed the question of the average Canadian farmer's financial position.
Mr. Chairman, a moment ago, I heard a government member outline the financial position of the farmer in regard to the rising prices of farm implements.
The problems of inflation and of rising prices in various fields have often been discussed here.

The farmer, who must necessarily renew his machinery, is faced with additional expenses when he comes to buy farm implements which are indispensable to him. That is why I believe he should be, to some extent, granted help similar to that extended more particularly to village dwellers who were able to obtain loans from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
In my opinion, the farmer could be granted assistance similar to that granted to citizens who want to set up what we often call a small industry. Our statutes include certain acts which authorize such loans, but the farmer has to rely on his own savings or on those of his family, or again on the good will of some of his friends who are able to lend him money, or still again obtain a loan from a caisse populaire or from a co-operative farm.
At this stage, Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that up to now the institution which probably helped our farmers the most, at least in northern Ontario, is undoubtedly the caisse populaire where, from time to time, they may obtain the necessary loans to help them carry on their production, and provide for the needs of their families.
However, I believe we should establish in this country a farmers' assistance program, so that our caisses populaires would not be the only ones to contribute to the progress of agricultural development.
We may well admire the work of those caisses populaires.
It is recognized that they have greatly helped the farmers, but still, I feel we should set up what the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) has termed an industrial expansion bank.
I think the time has come, as pointed out by the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska, to move towards the establishment of an agricultural expansion bank, bearing in mind particularly that the cost of farm implements is so high and that the cost of running a farm is constantly on the increase. Young farmers could certainly benefit from the establishment of such an expansion bank.
Mr. Chairman, I know that Canada's farmers have always appreciated price supports, which incidentally were established by the Liberal government. The Minister of Agriculture has stated in the house today that the support price on butter will be maintained at the same level. However, it

must be remembered that the present support price of 64 cents a pound is hardly better than the 58 cents price set by the Liberals a few years ago.
Before closing my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with my colleagues in urging the Minister of Agriculture to insure a closer check on over-production of certain goods in Canada.
I drew attention a moment ago, for instance, to the fact that the department now faces a problem because, in one particular field, farmers have been allowed to produce a 65 per cent surplus that only the stabilization board could absorb.
