Mr. Chairman, it is indeed a real privilege for me to say a few words at this time concerning the agricultural estimates. Waterloo county is one of Ontario's best agricultural centres and has produced outstanding livestock for many years; on many occasions our farmers have been prize winners at the Toronto exhibition and other prominent fairs. The A. Seiling farms in my home town, Elmira, Ontario, have produced many winners in top competitions. The Waterloo county federation of agriculture, incorporated in 1944, along with junior farmers and other organizations, have made a fine contribution to the welfare of the area and to the whole agricultural economy of our district. As a matter of fact, it has made a fine contribution to the whole of Canada.
One of our present concerns, however, is the limited facilities which are available for hog testing programs. The advanced registry and record of performance testing for swine has done a great deal to raise the standard. In 1934 a station was set up at New Hamburg, Ontario, on the advice of the advanced registry board. In 1938 a 48-pen piggery was opened at Waterloo in my riding. The building program for the advanced registry station was resumed after the second world war, and in 1948 a 60-pen piggery was constructed at the Waterloo station. At the present time the capacity of the Waterloo station is 112 pens. This is an institution which we are proud to have in our riding, and we all know the capable direction which Mr. Ken Cappin-dale has given it over the last few years.
However, the capacity of the present station at Waterloo appears to be inadequate. In the last few years particularly a considerable number of entries have had to be turned down because of the lack of sufficient facilities. I would strongly suggest to the government

that additional quarters be made available or that an entirely new and enlarged station be built.
It has played a most significant part in the breeding and selection of better hogs in the province of Ontario, and it must be increased in size to continue to fulfil this objective. Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Agriculture and his department have been ever ready to assist the Canadian farmer. With this in mind I would appreciate if this problem were given serious consideration at an early date.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words-I promise to make them brief-in connection with one or possibly two matters that are not in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. Before doing so I should like to compliment the Minister of Agriculture upon the way in which his department, and he personally, has helped me in my constituency on many problems. I want to say that there is no minister of the crown who has such a difficult position as the Minister of Agriculture. That is particularly true when you have people making such statements as we heard in the house this afternoon. One statement was so irresponsible that you would not think it could come from an hon. member of this house unless he in turn was on the lunatic fringe.
We have gone into various matters. I say "we" because it has been my privilege to sit and listen to certain members of the opposition and those in the far corner who have been making estimates and suggesting increases in the national budget. About every item which has been discussed involved an increase in expenditures. They suggested that such and such had to be increased, and then something else had to be increased, and if you summed up their entire suggestions and placed a monetary value on them you would find that their estimates would probably total in the neighbourhood of $4 billion additional added to a $6.6 billion budget. What can you think of such irresponsible suggestions coming from a group such as that? Would you think their suggestions are for the purpose of giving light to the Canadian people, or do they have a desire to lead astray?
In coming to the next point which I intend to make, that is the cost of farm machinery, the hon. member for Bow River touched on this point this afternoon and I want to elaborate somewhat on it. May I say that in talking with my constituents, the farmers, there is no problem which is more in their minds than the cost of farm machinery. I venture to say that I talked during Easter recess with some 40 or 50 farmers, and I cannot recall one conversation which did 66968-9-191
Business of the House
not include discussion about farm prices, and about all of those cost items entering into the farmers costs of production. These are the things you talk about when you sit down with a farmer and talk to him across his table over a cup of coffee.
The farmers invariably talked about the cost of farm machinery. The cost-price squeeze may come about as a result either of prices or costs. In other words, costs and prices are like the two blades of scissors; you cannot tell which one is doing the most cutting. So we have talked a lot about prices in the house but we have said little or nothing about costs. Costs are what the farmers are talking about, and I would suggest to the government that they give thorough consideration to the advisability of appointing of a royal commission to make a study of farm machinery costs. That analysis would not conflict with the price spread studies which are being made by Dr. Stewart because that particular investigation deals with the margins which are taken by different handlers of agricultural commodities. The commission which I am recommending would deal specifically with the cost of farm machinery, and I would also suggest to the government that in analysing those costs and hearing evidence they not only ask for evidence from machine companies but also from the farmers themselves.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, after all is said and done, the operation of this commission would focus attention on the most important problem facing the farmers in western Canada, and if it were properly handled and speedily executed it would clear the air and give the farmers an opportunity to see where they stand with respect to farm machinery costs. That commission would also recommend action which this parliament could follow in the next session. I therefore humbly suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that he give serious consideration to the creation of such a commission, and in closing I again wish to compliment the minister most sincerely in every respect on the way in which he has so ably handled the affairs of his department.
